newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Socialists raise stakes in "dirty war" row.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Socialists raise stakes in "dirty war" row.

text.p: Spain's Socialists raised the political stakes on Friday when they asked conservative Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar to state clearly whether his predecessor was to blame for a "dirty war" on Basque rebels.

The Socialists want to know if Aznar's number two had the government's backing when he directly blamed former Socialist prime minister Felipe Gonzalez at the weekend for the 1983-87 campaign of torture, kidnap and murder against ETA separatists.
"We want to know if it's his personal opinion or whether it has the support of the government," a Socialist spokeswoman told Reuters on Friday. "It's pretty serious."

The question will be put to Aznar, in power for five months, at parliamentary question time next Wednesday. Aznar, who has remained aloof from the latest skirmish, could choose not to answer -- but another minister would have to respond.

Deputy Prime Minister Francisco Alvarez Cascos, who controls Spain's secret services and has unrivalled access to top-secret information, set off the political storm last weekend when he accused Gonzalez himself of organising the GAL death squads.

Defence and victims' lawyers in the court probe into the Anti-Terrorist Liberation Groups (GAL) death squads, which killed nearly 30 people in the illegal campaign, immediately called Alvarez Cascos as a witness, saying he must know something.

"If he made these statements it would be because he has proof that Felipe Gonzalez and those near him in the government or in his circle could have participated in the activities of the GAL," an attorney representing victims, Teodoro Mota, said.
Aznar's Popular Party (PP) government, like its Socialist predecessors, has refused to hand over military intelligence files sought by the courts as proof of "dirty war" activities.

Several opposition parties have accused the PP, which came to power after a "clean hands" campaign, of striking a secret pact with the Socialists to cover up the past -- a theory shared by most Spaniards, according to opinion polls.
The PP now fears the Spanish public is beginning to associate it with the GAL.
Alvarez Cascos' decision to finger Gonzalez drew angry reactions from the Socialists, who called him a fascist and suggested he should be sacked and jailed.

The exchange of accusations has strained relations among Spain's two main political parties to the point of forcing Catalan powerbroker Jordi Pujol, whose coalition holds a key swing vote in parliament, to step in with a plea for peace.

Pujol said he feared a political crisis of the kind that led to the last general election in March could hurt Spain's chances of passing the tough 1997 budget needed in order to participate in a planned European Union single currency in 1999.

Gonzalez was forced into the March election more than a year ahead of schedule as a result of court charges that his former interior minister and other top Socialists had engineered and funded the "dirty war".
The Supreme Court has yet to decide whether it wants to question him.
Gonzalez, who has always denied any knowledge of the activities of the GAL, went further last week and said there had been no state terrorism under his 13-year administration.

It was in reply to this denial that Alvarez Cascos said what had happened had been "bodeguilla terrorism" -- a reference to the wine bar in the prime minister's residence where Gonzalez often entertained close friends.
